sections.html:
Lawrence Township sits in Mercer County between Trenton and Princeton. Before a house here changes owners, the township housing office has to inspect it, and that step carries its own application, fee and waiting period. Begin there, because it often takes longer than the rest of the paperwork combined.

The July 2025 population estimate is 34,165 on 21.73 square miles of land, up from 33,077 in the 2020 count. Most addresses carry a Lawrenceville mailing label, while some use Princeton or Trenton. Put the legal municipality, Lawrence Township, on any contract so the township's rules clearly apply regardless of the postal name.

Owners live in about two thirds of Lawrence homes. Median household income is $130,142, well above the $80,734 national figure, and a typical owner-held house is valued at $439,700. Rent and ownership costs sit close together: gross rent is about $2,020 a month and owners with a mortgage pay $2,933. The township has no rent control ordinance outside a short list of affordable-housing complexes.

Neighborhood names buyers search by include Slackwood, Eldridge Park, Colonial Lakelands, Port Mercer, Lawrence Station and Quaker Bridge, plus the historic village center of Lawrenceville. A September 2003 tornado followed Princeton Pike and damaged homes, so expect questions about roof age on houses along that corridor.

Buyers look at the commute first, and the average one-way trip is 28.7 minutes. Interstate 295 loops through the township and U.S. 1 splits it, while U.S. 206 (Lawrence Road) is the main local artery from Trenton to Princeton. County routes 533, 546 and 569 handle cross-town trips.

  • Rail: Northeast Corridor trains run along the eastern edge, with the nearest stations in Hamilton, Trenton, Princeton and Princeton Junction.
  • Bus: NJ Transit routes 600, 603, 605, 606, 609 and 613 serve Trenton, and route 612 is local.
  • Air: Trenton-Mercer Airport is in neighboring Ewing, and Philadelphia and Newark airports are about equally far.

Name the closest station and highway ramp when you describe the house to a buyer.

sections.h2: Certificate of Inspection for a sale
sections.html:
The housing office issues a Certificate of Inspection for sales, and the seller normally pays for and obtains it. It is a different document from a Certificate of Occupancy, which the Construction Official issues after new construction or a major renovation. The inspection certificate is needed before title passes, for condos and foreclosed properties too.

  • Cost and filing: $80 with the application, handed in at the office or mailed. Emailed forms and online payments are refused.
  • Scheduling: the office books a visit only after it holds the form and fee, and a slot usually opens within two weeks, though busy periods run longer.
  • Visit length: roughly 60 to 90 minutes for a house, about 30 for a condo or townhouse.
  • Validity: the certificate expires one year after the inspection. Return visits cost nothing.
  • Safety checks: alarms, detectors and extinguishers are examined in the same visit, so no separate certificate is issued.

A buyer can take on most violations by writing to the township, listing them and giving a repair date. Life safety items are different: they must be corrected and checked again before anyone lives there. A failed septic system or open permits fall to the seller to resolve before closing.

In an as-is or bank-owned sale the buyer may be the one to get the certificate, so settle that point in the contract. The township's Pre-Inspection Checklist lists the usual items, and walking through it a week before your visit gives you time to replace a dead smoke detector or fix a loose railing. The office does not expedite appointments, so call 609-844-7032 early to ask for the next open slot, since that date often sets the earliest possible closing.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Mercer County
sections.html:
The Mercer County Clerk, at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton, records Lawrence deeds. A regular deed costs $43 for page one and $10 for every page after that, and the public records room keeps weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30.

The seller pays the state's transfer fee. With a median near $439,700, many Lawrence sales fall under the schedule for prices over $350,000, and the rate rises in steps with the price. Deeds over $1 million recorded from July 10, 2025 onward carry a revised fee under a new state law, again paid by the seller.

The clerk accepts transfer fee payments only by cash, cashier's check, money order or an escrow account held by an attorney or business, and anything above $10,000 needs a certified or bank check. Closing attorneys and title agents usually arrange this on your behalf.

Lawrence buyers and their attorneys will want a short list of papers early, and most of it you already have.

  • The inspection application and fee receipt, then the certificate itself once issued.
  • Septic records if the house is not on sewer, since a failed system is the seller's problem to solve.
  • Permit history for decks, finished basements and additions, because open permits also fall to the seller.
  • Leases and deposit details for any tenant, along with a note on whether the buyer wants the house empty.
  • The latest tax bill and your mortgage payoff, so the closing attorney can total what comes out of your proceeds.

Handing this folder over with the contract keeps the closing on schedule.

A house in good shape with time for showings does well on the open market, given the Trenton and Princeton pull. A house needing repairs, occupied by tenants or facing a tight inspection date may suit an as-is cash purchase better. Whichever buyer you pick, get in writing who orders and pays for the Certificate of Inspection and how a failed item is handled.

A workable order of steps: book the inspection first, gather the survey, tax bill and any permit papers, compare written offers on price, closing date and fees, then let the closing attorney or title agent file the deed with the county clerk. A cash buyer removes the appraisal and bank approval, but the inspection certificate and recording still have to be finished before title passes, so start the township paperwork the day you decide to sell.

faqs.q: Is an inspection mandatory for a Lawrence Township sale?
faqs.a: Yes. A Certificate of Inspection must exist before title passes. It is normally the seller's job, costs $80 with the application, and lapses one year after the visit.

faqs.q: How soon can Lawrence Township inspect my house?
faqs.a: Usually within two weeks, though holidays and busy periods can stretch it. Appointments cannot be expedited, and the office books nothing until it holds the application and fee.

faqs.q: May a buyer assume inspection violations?
faqs.a: For most items, yes: the buyer writes to the township naming them and a fix date. Life safety violations still have to be corrected and re-inspected before move-in, and the seller must clear a failed septic system or open permits.

faqs.q: Which office takes a Lawrence deed for recording?
faqs.a: The Mercer County Clerk, 209 South Broad Street, Trenton. A deed costs $43 for the first page and $10 for each extra page.

faqs.q: Does Lawrence Township have rent control?
faqs.a: No, apart from a short list of affordable-housing complexes named by the housing office. Most single-family rentals and owner-occupied houses are not covered.
